newsitem.title: KENYA: Rwanda urges access for aid workers to Zaire camps.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda urges access for aid workers to Zaire camps.

text.p: Rwanda said on Thursday it was very concerned at the plight of nearly 100,000 Rwandan Hutu refugees in makeshift camps in Zaire and urged that aid workers be allowed to reach them.

"These are Rwandans we are talking about," said Joseph Bideri, spokesman for President Pasteur Bizimungu. "We are very concerned and would like to see NGOs (non-governmental organisations) and the United Nations have access."
Authorities in eastern Zaire have sealed off two camps south of Kisangani for four days amid reports of clashes between rebel forces, local villagers and refugees.

Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his forces stepped in only to stop attacks by refugees on local residents, but villagers reported on Tuesday that possibly hundreds of refugees had been killed by rebel troops.
Bideri dismissed as "cynical lies" suggestions that the Tutsi-dominated rebels -- backed by the Rwandan government -- were weeding out hardcore elements among the Hutu refugees.
The refugees are among the last of two million Hutus who fled to Zaire and Tanzania in 1994 to escape possible reprisals for their role in the genocide of 800,000 Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

Most returned at the end of last year in a repatriation sparked by Kabila's rebellion in eastern Zaire, but some 300,000 including former Rwandan troops and militiamen fled westwards to escape the advancing rebels.
Up to 100,000 stopped when they were overwhelmed by hunger, exhaustion and illness and overtaken by the rebels south of Kisangani, nearly 500 km (300 miles) from where they started.
"It is unfortunate they chose this option," Bideri told Reuters. "But I can only reiterate the Rwandan government position that we operate an open-door policy regarding those who want to return."

Bideri said Ephrahim Kabaija, chairman of Rwanda's national repatriation commission, was in Kisangani for talks with rebel authorities and aid agencies on the refugees. He said the government would explore every suggestion on how to speed up their repatriation.

Local authorities on Sunday ruled out a U.N-backed airlift for those remaining until at least May 5 for fear that a cholera outbreak in the camps could spread to Zairean villagers. The World Health Organisation has dismissed their fears as groundless.

The Rwandan government refused to allow the refugees to be airlifted directly from Kisangani to Rwanda's capital Kigali, saying they would overwhelm its main airport so should be flown to eastern Zaire's border with Rwanda and trucked in.
